title: Renewable deployment is accelerating, but technology and regional concentration shape who gains energy security
source_unit: International Renewable Energy Agency, Renewable Capacity Statistics 2026
geography: Global renewable power generation capacity, with regional and technology comparisons for 2016-2025 and detailed 2025 additions

denominator.unit: global renewable power capacity stock and annual additions

total_capacity.unit: GW of total renewable power capacity at end-2025

annual_growth.unit: percent annual increase in renewable capacity

share_of_total_additions.unit: percent of total global power-capacity expansion represented by renewables

observations.method: IRENA compilation of renewable power capacity installed and connected at year end using questionnaires, official national statistics, industry associations, reports, and news sources.
observations.uncertainty: Capacity is maximum net generating capacity, not electricity actually generated; reporting coverage, revisions, grid connection, and source quality vary across countries and technologies.
observations.subgroup: Utilities, governments, grid operators, investors, workers, households, firms, and communities affected by power-system investment and reliability.
observations.counterinterpretation: Rapid capacity growth does not by itself establish affordability, reliability, emissions reductions, access, or equitable local benefits.

denominator.unit: GW of renewable capacity added globally in 2025

solar_pv_component.unit: GW of solar photovoltaic capacity within solar additions

solar_wind_share.unit: percent of net renewable additions from solar and wind together

observations.method: IRENA technology-level accounting of annual additions across solar, wind, hydropower, bioenergy, geothermal, and off-grid systems.
observations.uncertainty: Technology shares describe nameplate capacity additions and do not measure dispatchability, storage, capacity factors, lifecycle impacts, or local system integration costs.
observations.subgroup: Solar and wind manufacturers, miners and material suppliers, grid planners, energy workers, consumers, and communities hosting generation and transmission.
observations.counterinterpretation: Concentration in solar and wind can reflect falling costs and rapid deployment while increasing the importance of storage, grids, flexibility, and complementary technologies.

observations.period: 2025; regional distribution of renewable capacity growth

denominator.unit: GW of global renewable capacity additions in 2025

asia_share.unit: percent of new renewable capacity contributed by Asia

asia_additions.unit: GW of renewable capacity added in Asia

asia_growth.unit: percent annual growth in Asia's renewable capacity

africa_additions.unit: GW added in Africa, its highest capacity increase in the series

middle_east_growth.unit: percent annual renewable-capacity growth in the Middle East

observations.method: IRENA regional aggregation of country-level renewable capacity statistics and annual additions.
observations.uncertainty: Regional aggregates can hide very different country baselines, access conditions, grid constraints, financing environments, and off-grid activity.
observations.subgroup: Regions and countries with different energy-import exposure, public finance, grid capacity, energy poverty, industrial capabilities, and climate vulnerabilities.
observations.counterinterpretation: High regional concentration may change as financing, supply chains, policy, and grid investment diffuse; current shares are not fixed geopolitical outcomes.

observations.period: 2025; regional capacity stock and energy-security gap

denominator.unit: GW of global renewable capacity at end-2025

asia_stock.unit: GW of renewable capacity in Asia

europe_stock.unit: GW of renewable capacity in Europe

central_america_caribbean_stock.unit: GW of renewable capacity in Central America and the Caribbean

security_implication.value: uneven renewable capacity leaves low-share economies more vulnerable and underscores the need to increase renewable energy for energy security

off_grid_additions.unit: GW of off-grid electricity capacity added outside Eurasia, Europe, and North America

observations.method: IRENA comparison of regional renewable capacity stocks, off-grid additions, and energy-security implications.
observations.uncertainty: Capacity stock is not equivalent to energy access or energy security; it does not identify prices, outages, ownership, local pollution, or household-level incidence.
observations.subgroup: Low-capacity regions, energy-importing states, off-grid communities, utilities, public agencies, and households exposed to unreliable or expensive energy.
observations.counterinterpretation: Small capacity stocks can coexist with strong potential, distributed systems, imports, efficiency, or other forms of energy resilience; aggregate capacity is one component of security.

related_sources.claim: IRENA's release provides the 2025 capacity highlights and regional interpretation.
IRENA's yearbook page provides the historical capacity-statistics series and datasets.

boundary: This record adds a renewable-deployment route across capacity growth, technology concentration, regional inequality, off-grid systems, and energy security. It uses aggregate IRENA capacity statistics, not respondent-level energy histories, individual utility bills, plant-level operating records, causal forecasts, or proof that capacity growth produces equal affordability or security for every place.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official IRENA publication and 2025 capacity highlights reviewed for total capacity, annual additions, technology composition, regional distribution, capacity stocks, off-grid additions, and energy-security interpretation.
